client: I've been really struggling lately with this huge group project I got assigned at university. There's going to be a final presentation in front of the whole class, and just thinking about it makes my chest tight and my mind go completely blank. I'm not sure talking about it is actually going to make the anxiety go away, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist:
Welcome, and I'm really glad you gave this a shot — it takes courage to reach out even when you're not sure it'll help. That tight feeling in your chest and your mind going blank are your body's very real responses to feeling threatened, and they make complete sense given how much pressure this situation feels like it carries. 

I'm curious — when you imagine that presentation, what's the specific thought or fear that seems to be at the center of it all for you?

client: Honestly, the thing that keeps running through my head is that everyone's going to see right through me — like they'll realize I don't actually know what I'm talking about and I've just been faking it this whole time. It's not even really about the presentation itself, it's more like... this fear that it'll be the moment everything falls apart and people finally figure out I don't belong there. And then I just feel this wave of guilt on top of it, like I should be more confident by now, I should have this together.
therapist:
What you're describing — that fear of being "found out" — is something many people experience, and it even has a name: impostor syndrome, which tells us this is a very common human experience rather than evidence that your fear is true. I also want to gently point out that you're carrying a double burden right now: the anxiety about the presentation *and* then judging yourself for feeling anxious, which can make everything feel so much heavier. 

Can you think of a moment, even a small one, where you actually *did* know what you were talking about — where your competence was real and visible?

client: I mean... yeah, I guess there was this one time a few months ago when a colleague asked me a really specific question about a project and I actually knew the answer right away, and they seemed genuinely impressed. But honestly, my first instinct when you asked that was to dismiss it — like, that was just luck, or it was a simple question anyone would know. I can see what you're trying to do with this exercise, but it's hard because my brain immediately finds a reason why those moments don't count.
therapist:
You just did something really insightful there — you caught your brain in the act of dismissing evidence, which is actually a huge step, because you can't challenge a pattern you can't see. That instinct to label your successes as "just luck" while treating your fears as absolute truth is a classic thinking pattern, and it's worth asking: if a close friend described that same moment of impressing a colleague, would you tell *them* it was just luck and didn't count?

What do you think it would feel like to hold that memory with even just a little more weight than your brain naturally wants to give it?

client: Honestly, if a friend told me that story, I'd probably say it was a big deal and they should feel proud. But when it's me, it just... feels different, like the rules change or something. I guess trying to hold onto that memory feels almost uncomfortable, like I'm being arrogant or setting myself up to be proven wrong later.
therapist:
That discomfort you're naming is so telling — your brain has learned to use humility as a kind of shield, as if staying small will protect you from disappointment or judgment. But there's an important difference between arrogance and simply being a fair witness to yourself, applying the same kindness to your own story that you'd so naturally offer a friend. 

What do you think taught you that believing in yourself was dangerous — where do you think that "different set of rules" for yourself might have come from?

client: I think it probably came from my family, honestly. Growing up, if you talked about yourself too positively, someone would always cut you down or make a joke at your expense, so I learned pretty quickly that it was safer to just... not. But hearing you frame it as "being a fair witness to myself" instead of arrogance, I don't know, that almost sounds too simple, like it can't really be that straightforward to just change something that's been wired in for that long.
therapist:
You're absolutely right that it's not simple — patterns built over years as a genuine survival strategy don't dissolve overnight, and I want to be honest with you about that rather than make it sound like a quick reframe fixes everything. But what you're describing isn't really about *changing* who you are; it's more like slowly, carefully updating a rule that made perfect sense for younger you but might be costing you something now. 

What would it mean for your life — maybe just in small, everyday moments — if you gradually stopped needing that shield quite as much?

client: I appreciate that you're being honest about it not being a quick fix, because honestly that's part of why I've been skeptical of therapy in the past. But when you ask what it would mean to not need that shield... I don't know, it's hard to even imagine, because the loneliness I feel now is bad, but at least it feels familiar and kind of safe. What if I let people in more and it just confirms what I already fear, that I'm too much, or not enough, or whatever?
therapist:
That tension you're describing — between the pain of loneliness and the fear that closeness might hurt even more — is one of the most human dilemmas there is, and it makes complete sense that your nervous system would rather choose a familiar ache over an uncertain risk. But I want to gently reflect something back: the belief that you're "too much or not enough" is something you've been protecting others from seeing, but it's also something that's never really been *tested* — the shield has been doing its job so well that you haven't had many chances to find out what people actually think when they see more of you. 

If you imagine one very small, low-stakes moment where you let someone see just a little more of the real you — not a grand gesture, just a tiny crack in the shield — what might that look like?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right that I haven't really tested it. But even thinking about a "tiny crack" makes my chest tighten, because what if that small moment is enough for someone to confirm what I already fear — that I really am too much? I guess if I had to think of something, maybe it would be admitting to my coworker that I had a rough week instead of just saying "I'm fine," but I'm already coming up with reasons why that's a bad idea.
therapist:
That example you came up with is actually really beautiful — it's honest, it's human, and it's exactly the kind of moment that could gently start to update that old rule, because telling someone you had a rough week isn't "too much," it's just being a person. And I notice you found the idea *and* immediately started arguing yourself out of it, which tells me part of you is genuinely ready to try even while another part is working hard to keep you safe. 

What are the reasons you're coming up with against it, and can we look at them together to see if they hold up?

client: Yeah, I guess the main thing I keep coming back to is that if I say "I had a rough week" and they respond with something dismissive — like just changing the subject or giving me some generic "oh that sucks" — I'll feel even more alone than if I'd said nothing at all. It's like the risk of that reaction feels worse than just staying quiet and keeping everything surface-level. And I know that probably sounds like I'm setting it up to fail before I even try, but I've been burned enough times that it doesn't feel irrational to me.
therapist:
Your caution isn't irrational at all — it's built from real experiences where opening up didn't go the way you needed it to, and that deserves to be honored rather than argued away. But I want to gently offer this: a dismissive "oh that sucks" would feel painful, yes, but you've already survived loneliness and disappointment many times — what you haven't yet had much chance to discover is whether connection is also possible. 

What if the goal of that small moment wasn't to get the perfect response from your coworker, but just to practice being honest and see that you can survive however they respond — would that feel any different?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it logically — like, yeah, I've survived bad responses before, so one more shouldn't break me. But there's something about framing it as "just practice" that feels a little hollow to me, like I'd be going in already bracing for failure instead of actually hoping for something real. I guess I'm scared that if I keep lowering my expectations enough to make connection feel "safe," I'll end up not really wanting it anymore.
therapist:
That's a profound and beautiful insight — you're not just afraid of being hurt, you're also afraid of losing the part of you that still genuinely *wants* connection, and that tells me that hope is still very much alive in you, even if it feels fragile. You're right that there's a difference between protecting yourself and slowly convincing yourself not to want things, and I don't want to help you build a smaller life — I want to help you find ways to want things and reach for them even when it's scary. 

So rather than "just practice," what would it look like to go into that moment with your coworker *actually hoping* for something real, while also knowing that whatever happens, it won't be the final verdict on whether connection is possible for you?

client: That question actually kind of stops me in my tracks, because I've never really thought about it that way — going in *hoping* for something real instead of just bracing for impact. But honestly, it feels almost dangerous to do that, like I'd be setting myself up to get hurt worse if it doesn't go well. I guess I'm not sure I know how to hold onto hope and also not let it crush me if the conversation just ends up being awkward and surface-level like usual.
therapist:
What you're describing - how to hold hope without being destroyed by disappointment - is honestly one of the deepest skills a person can develop, and the fact that you're asking that question so clearly means you're already thinking about this in a really mature way. I wonder if hope doesn't have to be all-or-nothing — not "this conversation will definitely give me what I need" but something softer, like "I am someone who deserves connection and I'm going to keep moving toward it, one imperfect moment at a time."

What would it feel like to think of hope less as a bet you place on one conversation, and more as a quiet commitment you make to yourself that you won't stop trying?
